name: Donnie Darko
blurb: Richard Kelly's cult film about a troubled teen told the world will end in 28 days
title: Donnie Darko Explained: Plot Summary and Ending
description: Donnie Darko explained: the characters, the full 28-day plot, the jet engine, Frank, the tangent universe and the main readings of the ending.
h1: Donnie Darko Explained: Plot, Characters and Ending
answer: Donnie Darko is a 2001 American film written and directed by Richard Kelly, his first feature, starring Jake Gyllenhaal. In October 1988, in a Virginia suburb, a troubled teenager sleepwalks out of his house and meets Frank, a figure in a grotesque rabbit costume, who tells him the world will end in 28 days. That same night a jet engine falls from the sky into his bedroom, and nobody can say where it came from. The film mixes high-school drama, 1980s suburban satire and time-travel science fiction, and its ending is one of the most argued-over of its era.

head: Character
Who they are
rows: Donnie Darko (Jake Gyllenhaal)
A bright, troubled high-school student who sleepwalks and sees visions
Frank
A man in a rabbit costume who appears to Donnie and gives him instructions
Gretchen Ross (Jena Malone)
A new student who has moved to town to hide from her violent stepfather; she and Donnie start dating
Rose and Eddie Darko (Mary McDonnell, Holmes Osborne)
Donnie's parents
Elizabeth and Samantha Darko (Maggie Gyllenhaal, Daveigh Chase)
Donnie's older sister, about to start college, and his little sister, a member of a dance troupe
Dr. Lillian Thurman (Katharine Ross)
Donnie's psychotherapist
Jim Cunningham (Patrick Swayze)
A motivational speaker whose fear-and-love programme is taught at Donnie's school
Kitty Farmer (Beth Grant)
A teacher devoted to Cunningham's programme
Karen Pomeroy and Dr. Kenneth Monnitoff (Drew Barrymore, Noah Wyle)
Donnie's English teacher and his physics teacher
Roberta Sparrow
An elderly local recluse known as Grandma Death, author of a book on time travel

body: Beginning. On the night of October 2, 1988, Donnie Darko sleepwalks outside, where Frank tells him that the world will end in 28 days, 6 hours, 42 minutes and 12 seconds. Donnie wakes the next morning on a golf course. When he gets home, a jet engine has crashed through the roof into his empty bedroom. Investigators cannot find any plane that lost one. Donnie, who is already on medication, is sent back to Dr. Thurman, who suspects paranoid schizophrenia.

Middle. Frank keeps appearing, and Donnie follows his instructions in a trance. He breaks a water main and floods the school, and an axe is left buried in the head of a bronze statue. School is cancelled, and Donnie walks Gretchen home; they begin dating. Donnie asks Dr. Monnitoff about time travel, and Monnitoff gives him The Philosophy of Time Travel, a book written by Roberta Sparrow. Donnie begins to see watery tunnels extending from people's chests, as if showing the paths they are about to take. At school he rebels against Kitty Farmer's lessons from Jim Cunningham's self-help programme and later insults Cunningham at an assembly. Karen Pomeroy, the one teacher who encourages him, is fired.

On the night of Samantha's dance performance, Frank directs Donnie to set fire to Cunningham's house. Firefighters find a hidden room containing child pornography, and Cunningham is arrested. Kitty Farmer, who wants to defend him in court, asks Rose to take her place as chaperone on the dance troupe's trip to Los Angeles, so Rose flies there with Samantha just before Halloween.

End. With their parents gone, Donnie and Elizabeth host a Halloween party. Gretchen arrives distraught because her mother has disappeared, and she and Donnie sleep together. Realising that Frank's deadline is only hours away, Donnie takes Gretchen and two friends to Roberta Sparrow's house. They run into two bullies, Seth and Ricky, who are robbing it, and a scuffle spills into the road. A car swerves to avoid the old woman and runs over Gretchen, killing her. The driver is Frank Anderson, Elizabeth's boyfriend, dressed in the rabbit costume he wore to the party. Donnie shoots him in the eye with his father's gun and carries Gretchen's body home.

A huge storm-like vortex forms over the town. Donnie drives Gretchen's body up to a ridge and watches as the plane carrying Rose and the dance troupe home is caught in it. One of its engines is torn off and sent back through time. The events of the past 28 days rewind, and it is again the night of October 2. This time Donnie is in bed, awake, laughing. The engine falls through the roof and kills him.

What the film shows: time rewinds to October 2 and Donnie dies in his bed when the engine falls, so none of the 28 days happened. In the morning, people in Donnie's life wake from troubled sleep as if from a bad dream; Frank touches his eye, and Cunningham is seen crying. Gretchen rides her bike past the Darko house, where neighbours have gathered. She has never met Donnie, but she and Rose exchange a wave as if they half recognise each other.

The film never states its rules. Most explanations come from Roberta Sparrow's book, The Philosophy of Time Travel, whose pages were published by Kelly in The Donnie Darko Book (2003) and included in the 2004 director's cut. Commentators, including a widely read Salon explainer built on the book and Kelly's DVD commentary, describe the main reading like this:

ul: On October 2 an unstable copy of reality, a Tangent Universe, opened around the town. Its extra object, the Artifact, is the jet engine.
If the Artifact is not sent back to the Primary Universe within 28 days, the Tangent Universe collapses into a black hole and destroys everything.

Donnie is the Living Receiver, given strength and foresight to send it back. The people around him are the Manipulated Living, nudging him toward his task; those who die in the Tangent Universe, Frank and Gretchen, become the Manipulated Dead, who can travel through time and set a trap that leaves him no other choice.
By sending the engine back from his mother's plane, Donnie saves the world; by staying in bed, he accepts the death he escaped on October 2.

body: Other readings are also common, and the question is debated. One is psychological: Donnie is mentally ill, the visions are hallucinations, and the film is about a lonely, frightened boy choosing to die for the people he loves. Another is religious: Donnie is a Christ-like figure sacrificing himself, a reading Salon finds supported in Kelly's commentary. The theatrical cut leaves room for all of these; the director's cut, which shows pages of the book on screen, pushes much more strongly toward the science-fiction explanation. Kelly has said he did not want to explain the ending further, feeling that more explanation would make the film collapse under its own pretension.

ul: Sacrifice: Donnie ends the film by giving up his life so that Gretchen, his mother and sister, and everyone else can live.
Fate versus free will: Frank's orders and the book's rules suggest Donnie is being steered, yet his last laugh suggests a choice made freely.
Loneliness and death: Roberta Sparrow's warning that every creature dies alone haunts Donnie, and the ending answers it with a death he chooses calmly.
Suburban hypocrisy: Cunningham's fear-and-love slogans and Kitty Farmer's zeal are exposed by the discovery in his house.
Adolescence and mental illness: the film takes Donnie's medication and therapy seriously and never fully separates his illness from his gift.
Runtime: 113 minutes (theatrical cut, 2001). The director's cut (2004) adds about 20 minutes of footage, on-screen pages from The Philosophy of Time Travel and changes to the music.
Which version: the theatrical cut is more mysterious; the director's cut explains more. Many fans prefer to see the theatrical version first.
Content: rated R in the US; includes gun violence, a death by car, strong language and references to child abuse.
A sequel, S. Darko (2009), was made without Kelly's involvement and is not needed to understand the original.

check.q: What falls into Donnie's bedroom on the night of October 2?
check.why: A jet engine crashes through the roof while Donnie is out sleepwalking, and no plane is found that lost one.

check.q: Who is the Frank who kills Gretchen with his car?
options: Elizabeth's boyfriend, in a rabbit costume
check.why: Frank Anderson, Elizabeth's boyfriend, is driving home from the Halloween party in his rabbit costume.

options: He is killed in the plane crash
The jet engine falls on him in his bed after time rewinds
check.why: After the engine is sent back through the vortex, it is October 2 again and Donnie stays in his bed as it falls.

faq.q: What is the tangent universe in Donnie Darko?
faq.a: In Roberta Sparrow's book, it is an unstable copy of reality that lasts 28 days and must be closed by sending its extra object, the jet engine, back to the real universe before it collapses.

faq.q: Should I watch the theatrical cut or the director's cut of Donnie Darko?
faq.a: The 2001 theatrical cut is shorter and leaves more to interpretation; the 2004 director's cut adds about 20 minutes and text from The Philosophy of Time Travel that spells out the time-travel rules.

faq.q: Why does Frank wear a rabbit costume?
faq.a: In the story it is simply his Halloween costume, worn on the night Donnie shoots him; Donnie sees this future version of him from the start. Commentators often link the rabbit to Alice in Wonderland, another story about following a rabbit into a world with strange rules.
